Dear NicheMapR users,

I've been playing around with the microclimate() function to predict the body temperature of intertidal mussels (Mytilus spp.).
The idea is to show that the orientation of mussels is a better predictor of body temperature than the topography of the shore.
To do so, I ran the model for all possible combinations of slope and azimuth during (i) the period I have in-situ temperature data for (2017-08-01 to 2017-09-13) and (ii) longer periods (>1 year) that will serve as a baseline for further analyses.
My research question involves two types of mussels: a dark one (albedo=0.1) and a lighter one (albedo=0.2).

The function works well for some combinations of slope and azimuth but it fails systematically under a specific range of slope and azimuth (around azimuth=280° and slope=80°) and it gets worse when the model is run for extended periods (see figure attached).
My example here is a for a site located close to Vilamoura, Portugal (longitude=-8.122935, latitude=37.070756) but I find the same pattern of failures (i.e., for azimuth>180° and slope>0°) for my nine other sites (Portugal, France and United Kingdom).

Could you help me figure out what goes wrong?

Here is my code (hourly weather data, from ECMWF's ERA5 global climate reanalysis, are attached):

Hi Jonathan,

I just had a quick look through and it is probably because of the density you're using - it's much too low (lower than air!). That would be resulting in very high temperatures at times, I'm guessing. The units are megagrams / m3 which is the same as g / cm3, so mussels would be something close to water, i.e. a value of 1. You might want to specify different thermal properties for different layers in the soil, e.g. top 6 cm could be the properties of mussels and then rock from there down.

Note also that the roughness height isn't the height of the object, but a more abstract notion. The value you have is fine, but I just noted that you were linking it to the height of the mussels so I thought I'd better flag it.

Let me know if changing the density fixes the problem.

All the best,
Mike

Hi Jonathan,

That zenith angle algorithm isn't giving you hourly zenith angles but rather it seems just the minimum ones for a day. It should go to below 90 at night (i.e. below the horizon). I think this what is now causing you problems. Below I've pasted an algorithm I found somewhere, that I use for some of my simulations, and it makes your simulation run. Make sure you get the time zone right for the time vector you put into the algorithm though.

Hopefully this does the trick.

All the best,
Mike
SZA <- function(timein = Sys.time(), Lat = 50.910335, Lon = 11.568740){
  # Calculate solar zenith angle
  # according to http://solardat.uoregon.edu/SolarRadiationBasics.html
  # calculations have been modified for positive East longitudes and time in UTC
  # Extract time information
  #( hour, minute, second, dummy, n ) = time.gmtime()[3:8]
  # Calculate declination of the sun d
  #if (is.vector(timein)){
 
  sza <- vector("numeric", length=length(timein))
  for(i in 1:length(timein)){
    time <- as.POSIXlt(timein[i], tz = 'GMT')
    d2r <- pi / 180
    r2d <- 1/d2r
    d <- 23.45 * d2r * sin(d2r *360 *(284 + time$yday) / 365) # [rad]
    #print (sprintf("d = %f", d * 180 / pi))
    # Calculate equation of time
    if (time$yday <= 106){
      E_qt <- -14.2 * sin(pi * (time$yday + 7) / 111)      # Eq. SR.4a [minutes]
    }else{if (time$yday<= 166){
      E_qt <-   4.0 * sin(pi * (time$yday - 106) / 59)     # Eq. SR.4b [minutes]
    }else{if (time$yday<= 246){
      E_qt <-  -6.5 * sin(pi * (time$yday - 166) / 80)     # Eq. SR.4c [minutes]
    }else{E_qt <-  16.4 * sin(pi * (time$yday - 247) / 113)}}}    # Eq. SR.4d [minutes]
    # Get UTC time T
    T <- time$hour + time$min / 60 + time$sec / 3600 # [hours]
    # Calculate solar time T_solar (East longitudes are positive!)
    Longitude <- Lon#*d2r
    T_solar <- T + Longitude / 15 + E_qt / 60 # [hours]
    # Calculate hour angle w (positive: from midnight to noon, negative: from noon to midnight)
    w <- pi * (12 - T_solar) / 12 # [rad]
    # Calculate solar zenith angle Z
    l <- Lat * d2r # [rad]
    if(class(Lat)[1] == "RasterLayer"){
      if(i == 1){
        sza1 <- 90 - asin(sin(l) * sin(d) + cos(l) * cos(d) * cos(w)) * r2d # [deg]
        sza1[sza1 > 90] <- 90
        sza <- sza1
      }else{
        sza1 <- 90 - asin(sin(l) * sin(d) + cos(l) * cos(d) * cos(w)) * r2d # [deg]
        sza1[sza1 > 90] <- 90
        sza <- stack(sza, sza1)
      }
    }else{
      sza[i] <- 90 - asin(sin(l) * sin(d) + cos(l) * cos(d) * cos(w)) * r2d # [deg]
    }
  }
  #}
  return(sza)
}

parts:
Hi Jonathon,

The ERR parameter is controlling when the numerical integrator is satisfied with its solution of the heat budget - by increasing it you're getting a less accurate calculation so ideally you keep it as low as possible. Five isn't too out there, but I have rarely needed to alter it from the default of 1.5 except in the case of simulating snow, suggesting something's awry. I just scanned your parameters again, though, and you have 2800 g/cm2 for the density of the rock - that could well be the problem (should be 2.8). The other thing that would be worth doing is a check against e.g. the output of micro_ncep for a particular site, with default settings and then gradually trying to make it come closer to your specific settings, to make sure it's all looking ok. Check carefully how the plots of soil temp. vs. time look as you go to make sure nothing weird is going on. Always good to start from somewhere that you have confidence is working properly, and then modify gradually. It's so easy for issues to creep in with this kind of modelling.

All the best,
Mike
